oque.text: SaniPLAN is an Open Source simulation model, adjustable to local conditions, developed in Excel and sponsored by the IDB, to support the preparation of National or Regional Sanitation Investment Plans.

ato0.title: How much does it cost to achieve universal urban sanitation in the Dominican Republic?

s1.title: A model at the center
items: SaniPLAN calculates the investment required to reach a coverage target.
Spatial data generate the parameters for each district.
The results show where the needs are and what they cost.

s2.title: We start with the data
items: Censuses, satellite imagery, streets, buildings and network records.
Each source has a different level of aggregation.
Spatial analysis turns these sources into indicators by district.

ato1.title: Spatial data
ato1.lead: A national plan depends on where people live, how the city is built and where service already exists.

fontes.title: Sources and levels of aggregation
items: Each dataset exists at a different level. A district has, on average, 1,240 hexagons; a province, 12 districts; the country, 32 provinces.
Population is available at fine scale. Sewer coverage, only by province. Treatment, only as a national average.
The result is never more precise than the most aggregated data used in the calculation.
fontes.note: Solid hexagon = level at which the data exist; the lighter ones, to the right, are possible aggregations. Hollow dot = partial data (only in some districts).
fontes.hint: Hover over a level in the table to see it on the map. Next, we zoom in on Santo Domingo Este.

sdeDm.title: One value per district
items: The census reports population by district: the value applies to the whole polygon, including empty areas.
Santo Domingo Este: 961,844 inhabitants in 131 km².

sdeHex.title: The same population, by 10-ha hexagon
items: The census population is distributed across the hexagons where there are buildings. The district total is preserved.
What changes is knowing where people are.
Hexagons have the same area everywhere in the country and 6 equidistant neighbors, which makes it easier to detect urban continuity.
486,526 hexagons cover the country; 1,311 in Santo Domingo Este.
sdeHex.hint: Click a hexagon to see its indicators.

censo.title: Improving the available data
items: Between 2010 and 2022 the country's rural population grew by about 550,000, against the urbanization trend.
In Santo Domingo Este, the rural population went from 40,099 to 116,935 (+192%).
Blue: official urban area. Orange: area that the census classifies as rural.
The imagery shows why: the area classified as rural has been urbanized.
censo.swipe: Drag the slider to compare 2010 and 2022

reclass.title: Reclassifying what is already city
items: Orange: hexagons outside the official urban area, with more than 100 buildings and at least 50% of neighbors built up.
On the 2022 imagery, the street and block pattern appears where the census records rural area.
In Santo Domingo Este: 148 hexagons, ~100,000 inhabitants and 23,944 buildings now count as urban.
Nationwide, the urban population considered is 860,000 above the census.
reclass.hint: Click a hexagon to see buildings, streets and population.

sdeRuas.title: From streets and buildings to network length per connection
items: Street length (OpenStreetMap) is a good proxy for the length of the sewer network.
The number of buildings (Overture Maps) is a good proxy for the number of connections.
In each urban hexagon: street meters ÷ buildings. Adding up the hexagons, each district gets its own value. Santo Domingo Este: 12.7 m per connection.
As a result, the network cost per connection is no longer a single average: dense districts and sparsely built districts get different costs.

media.title: Network length per connection is not the same everywhere
items: The same calculation, repeated across the 18,352 urban hexagons of the country.
In dense cores, a few meters of network serve one connection. In sparsely built areas, many more are needed.
Investment plans usually adopt one average value for the whole country. Here, the value varies from district to district, and so does the cost per connection.
media.hint: Each dot is a 10-ha urban hexagon. Zoom in to see the hexagons and click to see streets and buildings.

indic.title: The indicators that feed the model
items: The spatial analysis ends with a set of indicators for each of the 393 districts.

Network length and households per connection come from the urban hexagons. Sewer coverage exists only by province and is adjusted by district; where network records exist, the population served was recalculated within the network area.
Treatment: national average of ~50% of the wastewater collected.
These values feed into SaniPLAN for each district.
indic.hint: Choose an indicator above the map and click a district to see the values.

pob.title: Population projection
pob.lead: For the study carried out for the Dominican Republic, population projections were developed for each district from historical census data and population growth curves, adjusted to the official ONE projections.

methods.title: Methods
items: Logistic: grows toward a saturation population.
Decreasing rate: growth that slows over time.
Gompertz: asymmetric S-curve; the most used (374 districts).
Linear: constant increment per year.
Geometric: constant rate per year.

calib.title: National calibration
items: The sum of the districts was adjusted year by year to the official national projection (ONE).
Urbanization: 86.88% of the total population in 2040.
Baseline: 8,875,227 urban inhabitants in 2024.

chart.hint: Hover over the chart to read the values.

custos.title: Unit costs
custos.lead: For the study carried out for the Dominican Republic, the following unit costs were adopted, already converted to country costs.

rede.title: Sewer network
items: Two types: conventional (AC) and simplified (AE).
Three levels of construction difficulty: low, medium, high. In the metropolitan district, always high.
Cost per connection = m of network per connection × $/m + house connection + transport factor (trunk sewers, pumping).
Densification (infill): 10% of new connections are served by the existing network (−10%).
m of network per connection and households per connection come from the spatial analysis (Part 2).
head: Difficulty
AC network $/m
AE network $/m
AC house conn. $/conn.
AE house conn. $/conn.
rede.photoAC: Conventional network: deep trenches, larger-diameter pipes.
rede.photoAE: Simplified (condominial) network: shallow, small-diameter pipes, short house connections.
rede.desglose: Breakdown of the unit cost per meter (services, materials, indirect costs), basis of the cost module.

ete.title: Treatment
items: Cost curves for wastewater treatment plants as a function of influent BOD load and the intended level of treatment.
Four curves, one for each standard treatment level (BOD removal): primary, basic, intermediate and advanced.
Curves based on costs of WWTPs built in Latin America and the Caribbean.
In compliance with Dominican Republic environmental legislation, BOD removals of 85% to 88% were considered for inland areas and 67% to 77% for the coastal region.
A per capita load varying with the population of the district was considered, from 40 to 60 g BOD/inhab·day.
ete.credit: Curves: wastewater treatment plant unit-cost module developed by consultant Dr. Konrad Buchauer (2024).

emis.title: Submarine outfall
items: Six coastal districts with more than 100,000 inhabitants: Puerto Plata, Bajos de Haina, La Romana, San Pedro de Macorís, Santo Domingo de Guzmán and Santo Domingo Este.
Cost per meter as a function of diameter, estimated from population; added to the WWTP cost per inhabitant.
